src/flask/app.py:128:
src/flask/app.py:129:    .. admonition:: About the First Parameter
src/flask/app.py:130:
src/flask/app.py:131:        The idea of the first parameter is to give Flask an idea of what
src/flask/app.py:132:        belongs to your application.  This name is used to find resources
src/flask/app.py:133:        on the filesystem, can be used by extensions to improve debugging
src/flask/app.py:134:        information and a lot more.
src/flask/app.py:135:
src/flask/app.py:136:        So it's important what you provide there.  If you are using a single
src/flask/app.py:137:        module, `__name__` is always the correct value.  If you however are
src/flask/app.py:138:        using a package, it's usually recommended to hardcode the name of
src/flask/app.py:139:        your package there.
src/flask/app.py:140:
src/flask/app.py:141:        For example if your application is defined in :file:`yourapplication/app.py`
src/flask/app.py:142:        you should create it with one of the two versions below::
src/flask/app.py:143:
src/flask/app.py:144:            app = Flask('yourapplication')
src/flask/app.py:145:            app = Flask(__name__.split('.')[0])
src/flask/app.py:146:
src/flask/app.py:147:        Why is that?  The application will work even with `__name__`, thanks
src/flask/app.py:148:        to how resources are looked up.  However it will make debugging more
src/flask/app.py:149:        painful.  Certain extensions can make assumptions based on the
src/flask/app.py:150:        import name of your application.  For example the Flask-SQLAlchemy
src/flask/app.py:151:        extension will look for the code in your application that triggered
src/flask/app.py:152:        an SQL query in debug mode.  If the import name is not properly set
src/flask/app.py:153:        up, that debugging information is lost.  (For example it would only
src/flask/app.py:154:        pick up SQL queries in `yourapplication.app` and not
src/flask/app.py:155:        `yourapplication.views.frontend`)

src/flask/ctx.py:158:

src/flask/ctx.py:160:
src/flask/ctx.py:161:        Due to the following caveats, it is often safer (and simpler) to pass
src/flask/ctx.py:162:        the data you need when starting the task, rather than using this and
src/flask/ctx.py:163:        relying on the context objects.
src/flask/ctx.py:164:
src/flask/ctx.py:165:    In order to avoid execution switching partially though reading data, either
src/flask/ctx.py:166:    read the request body (access ``form``, ``json``, ``data``, etc) before
src/flask/ctx.py:167:    starting the task, or use a lock. This can be an issue when using threading,

src/flask/ctx.py:169:
src/flask/ctx.py:170:    If the task will access ``session``, be sure to do so in the parent as well
src/flask/ctx.py:171:    so that the ``Vary: cookie`` header will be set. Modifying ``session`` in
src/flask/ctx.py:172:    the task should be avoided, as it may execute after the response cookie has
src/flask/ctx.py:173:    already been written.
